stem: Which accounting concept requires revenue and expenses to be recorded in the period in which they arise, whether or not cash has moved?

options.rationale: Correct: costs and revenue are assigned to the period they belong to.
Historical cost concerns the amount at which assets are first recorded.
The entity concept separates the owner from the business.
Going concern assumes the business will continue; it does not time revenue and costs.

explanation: Adjustments for accruals, prepayments and depreciation all apply the matching (accruals) concept.

stem: Goods costing US\$250 are taken by the owner for personal use. Which entry is made?

options.rationale: Correct: drawings rise by the cost and purchases fall by the same amount.
This reverses the correct entry.
The goods were not sold, so no revenue arises.
Closing inventory is counted, so it is not changed.

explanation: The goods are removed from purchases at cost and charged to the owner as drawings.

stem: Which year-end adjustment increases profit for the year?

options.rationale: An accrual raises expenses and reduces profit.
Depreciation is an expense, so profit falls.
Correct: part of the premium belongs to next year, so this year's expense falls.

options.content: An increase in the allowance for irrecoverable debts
options.rationale: The increase is an expense, so profit falls.

explanation: A prepayment reduces the expense of the year, so profit rises.

stem: Depreciation of equipment has not been charged. What is the effect on the draft financial statements?

options.content: Profit is overstated and the carrying amount of equipment is understated
options.rationale: Without the charge the carrying amount is too high, not too low.

options.content: Profit is understated and the carrying amount is overstated
options.rationale: Missing an expense overstates profit.

options.content: Profit is understated and the carrying amount is understated
options.rationale: Both are overstated when depreciation is missing.

options.content: Profit and the carrying amount of equipment are both overstated
options.rationale: Correct: the expense is missing and the asset has not been reduced.

explanation: Depreciation is an expense and reduces the asset's carrying amount, so omitting it overstates both.

stem: A computer costing US\$1,200 was bought in the year and debited to repairs. No depreciation is yet charged on it. What is the effect on the draft profit before depreciation is considered?

options.content: Profit is overstated by US\$1,200 and non-current assets are overstated by US\$1,200
options.rationale: Charging the cost as an expense lowered profit, not raised it.

options.content: Profit is understated by US\$1,200 and current assets are overstated
options.rationale: No current asset is involved.

options.content: Profit is correct but non-current assets are understated
options.rationale: Profit is understated too because repairs are overcharged.

options.content: Profit is understated by US\$1,200 and non-current assets are understated by US\$1,200
options.rationale: Correct: the expense was too high and the asset was omitted.

explanation: A capital item charged as an expense understates profit and leaves the asset out of the statement of financial position.
hints: Was an expense overstated or understated?

stem: Trade receivables were US\$24,000 before a write-off of US\$1,000. The allowance for irrecoverable debts is to be 5% of the remaining receivables. The allowance was US\$900 at the start of the year. What is the total charge for irrecoverable debts in the statement of profit or loss?

options.rationale: The whole allowance has been charged instead of its increase.
This is the allowance required, not the charge.
The write-off has been left out.

explanation: Remaining receivables 23,000; allowance 5% = 1,150; increase 250; charge 1,000 + 250 = 1,250.
hints: Find the receivables remaining, then the allowance, then its change.

stem: In an extended trial balance, the profit for the year is the balancing figure. Where is it entered?

options.content: Credit side of both pairs of columns
options.rationale: Profit cannot be credited in both pairs.

options.content: Debit side of both pairs of columns
options.rationale: The financial position columns need a credit for capital.

options.content: Debit side of the profit or loss columns and credit side of the financial position columns
options.rationale: Correct: it clears the profit and loss account and increases capital.

options.content: Credit side of the profit or loss columns and debit side of the financial position columns
options.rationale: This would be the entry for a loss.

explanation: Credits exceed debits in the profit or loss columns, so profit is added to the debit side; the same amount is a credit in the financial position columns (capital).
hints: Income exceeds expenses in the profit or loss columns.

stem: A trader took goods costing US\$500 for personal use but debited drawings and credited sales with their selling price of US\$650. What is the effect on profit for the year?

options.rationale: Revenue was increased, so profit is not understated.
Correct: sales are 650 higher but purchases should only be 500 lower.
Part of the credit (500) is the correct reduction in cost; only the difference is the error.
500 is the correct reduction in purchases, not the error.

explanation: The correct credit is purchases 500; the credit made was sales 650. Profit is 150 too high.
hints: Compare the credit made with the credit that should have been made.

stem: An increase in the allowance for irrecoverable debts reduces profit for the year.
explanation: True. The increase is charged as an expense. A decrease in the allowance is added back and raises profit.

stem: Goods taken by the owner for personal use must be deducted from the closing inventory figure.
explanation: False. The closing inventory is counted physically, so goods already taken are not in it. The entry reduces purchases and increases drawings.
hints: Closing inventory is counted at the year end.

stem: Match each adjustment to its double entry.

left.content: Wages owing at the year end

right.content: Debit depreciation expense; credit accumulated depreciation

explanation: Each entry pairs a statement of profit or loss account with a statement of financial position account (drawings affect capital).

stem: Complete the sentence on accrued wages.

payload.template: Wages owing at the year end {{blank:a}} profit and are shown within {{blank:b}}.

explanation: An accrued expense is added to the expense, which reduces profit, and the unpaid amount is a current liability.

stem: Name the account credited, other than the asset account, when a fixed charge for depreciation is recorded in the books.
explanation: The charge is debited to the depreciation expense account and credited to accumulated depreciation (provision for depreciation).

stem: Draft profit for the year was US\$18,200. Rent owing of US\$430 and depreciation of US\$1,650 were not recorded, and insurance prepaid of US\$270 and commission receivable of US\$85 were also omitted. Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
explanation: 18,200 - 430 (rent owing) + 270 (prepayment) - 1,650 (depreciation) + 85 (commission earned) = 16,475. The first wrong answer reverses every sign.
workedSolution: 1. 18,200 - 430 (rent owing) + 270 (prepayment) - 1,650 (depreciation) + 85 (commission earned) = 16,475. The first wrong answer reverses every sign.

stem: Trade receivables were US\$40,000 before an irrecoverable debt of US\$2,000 was written off. The allowance for irrecoverable debts is to be 4% of the remaining receivables; it stood at US\$2,100 at the start of the year. Calculate the net charge for irrecoverable debts in the statement of profit or loss.
explanation: Remaining receivables 38,000; allowance 4% = 1,520; decrease 2,100 - 1,520 = 580. Net charge = 2,000 - 580 = 1,420.
workedSolution: 1. Remaining receivables 38,000; allowance 4% = 1,520; decrease 2,100 - 1,520 = 580. Net charge = 2,000 - 580 = 1,420.
hints: The allowance falls, so part of the write-off is offset.

stem: Draft profit for the year was US\$12,400. Later it was found that (i) goods costing US\$180 had been taken by the owner and no entry made, and (ii) a machine costing US\$1,500 had been debited to repairs; it is to be depreciated at 10% for the year. Calculate the corrected profit.
explanation: 12,400 + 180 (purchases reduced) + 1,500 (repairs overstated) - 150 (depreciation 10% of 1,500) = 13,930. Forgetting the depreciation gives 14,080.
workedSolution: 1. 12,400 + 180 (purchases reduced) + 1,500 (repairs overstated) - 150 (depreciation 10% of 1,500) = 13,930. Forgetting the depreciation gives 14,080.

stem: Draft profit was US\$15,000. Wages owing US\$700, rent prepaid US\$240 and depreciation US\$1,800 had not been recorded, and goods costing US\$350 taken by the owner had not been recorded (they were bought in the year and are in purchases). Opening capital was US\$24,000 and the owner's drawings in cash were US\$5,200. Calculate the closing capital.
explanation: Corrected profit = 15,000 - 700 + 240 - 1,800 + 350 = 13,090; closing capital = 24,000 + 13,090 - 5,200 - 350 = 31,540. Omitting the 350 added to profit gives 31,190; using the draft profit gives 33,800.
workedSolution: 1. Corrected profit = 15,000 - 700 + 240 - 1,800 + 350 = 13,090; closing capital = 24,000 + 13,090 - 5,200 - 350 = 31,540. Omitting the 350 added to profit gives 31,190; using the draft profit gives 33,800.
hints: Correct the profit first; own-use goods raise profit and are also drawings.

stem: Explain why every year-end adjustment must be entered twice.

points.description: Double entry: each adjustment changes a statement of profit or loss account and a statement of financial position account (or capital)
Entering it once would leave profit or the financial position wrong and the statement of financial position out of balance

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Under double entry every change has two sides. An accrual, for example, raises an expense and creates a liability. If only one side is entered the statement of financial position will not balance and profit or net assets will be misstated.

explanation: One mark for the two-sided nature, one for the consequence of a one-sided entry.

stem: Explain how the prudence concept affects the allowance for irrecoverable debts.

points.description: Receivables should not be shown at more than the amount expected to be collected
An allowance is deducted from receivables and the increase is charged as an expense
Profit is therefore not overstated by debts that are unlikely to be paid

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prudence says assets and profit should not be overstated. The business estimates the receivables it will not collect and deducts an allowance, and the increase in the allowance is charged to the statement of profit or loss, so profit is not inflated by doubtful debts.

explanation: Link prudence to the lower profit and lower receivables figure.
hints: Think of what happens to the profit if no allowance is made.

stem: Before applying for a bank loan, Nyasha proposes reducing the depreciation rate on her vehicles from 20% to 10% so that profit looks higher. Evaluate her proposal.

points.description: A lower rate raises profit and the carrying amount, which may impress the bank
A rate change is acceptable only if the useful life has genuinely changed, otherwise profit is overstated (breach of prudence and neutrality)
Consistency: methods should not change simply to improve results; the bank may detect this and lose trust
Judgement: reject unless the vehicles' real useful life has lengthened, and disclose any change

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The change would raise profit and the carrying amount of the vehicles, which might help the application. But depreciation should reflect real use, so a lower rate is justified only if the vehicles will last longer. Otherwise profit is overstated, the accounts are not neutral and the bank may lose trust if it finds out. I would reject the proposal unless the useful life has truly changed, and disclose any change.

explanation: One mark per reasoned point; the last mark is for a supported judgement.
hints: Who uses the statements, and are the estimates honest?

stem:
Tatenda owns a hardware shop in Mutare. The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was US\$22,600. These adjustments have not been made:

| No. | Adjustment |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Equipment costing US\$36,000 is to be depreciated at 12.5% of cost. |
| 2 | An irrecoverable debt of US\$800 is to be written off from trade receivables of US\$21,000. |
| 3 | The allowance for irrecoverable debts is to be 3% of the remaining trade receivables; the allowance is US\$450 at present. |
| 4 | Rent of US\$350 was received in advance for next year but credited to rent received for this year. |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the increase in the allowance for irrecoverable debts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.explanation: 22,600 - 4,500 - 800 - 156 - 350 = 16,794. The rent received in advance must be deducted from this year's income.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 22,600 - 4,500 - 800 - 156 - 350 = 16,794. The rent received in advance must be deducted from this year's income.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Where is the rent received in advance shown in the statement of financial position?

options.rationale: It is not an amount due to the business.
Correct: the business owes the tenant the use of the premises.
It is neither non-current nor an asset.
It is not the owner's investment.

parts.explanation: Income received in advance is a current liability.

explanation: This item tests depreciation, the allowance for irrecoverable debts and income received in advance.
hints: Remember that the rent received in advance is deducted from profit, not added.
Calculate the allowance after the write-off.

stem:
The trial balance of Chipo Mutasa's trading business in Masvingo is below. The statements are for internal use.

**Trial balance at 31 December 2025**

| Account | Debit US\$ | Credit US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Equipment at cost | 32,000 |  |
| Accumulated depreciation |  | 7,500 |
| Inventory at 1 January 2025 | 8,900 |  |
| Purchases | 70,600 |  |
| Sales |  | 121,400 |
| Wages | 16,100 |  |
| Rent | 5,100 |  |
| Insurance | 2,160 |  |
| Trade receivables | 15,200 |  |
| Allowance for irrecoverable debts |  | 540 |
| Bank | 5,900 |  |
| Trade payables |  | 8,300 |
| Drawings | 8,400 |  |
| Capital at 1 January 2025 |  | 26,620 |
| **Total** | **164,360** | **164,360** |

Adjustments at 31 December 2025:

| No. | Adjustment |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Closing inventory is US\$12,300. |
| 2 | Wages owing are US\$1,260. |
| 3 | Insurance prepaid is US\$540. |
| 4 | Depreciate the equipment at 10% of cost. |
| 5 | Write off an irrecoverable debt of US\$690. |
| 6 | The allowance is to be 4% of the remaining trade receivables. |
| 7 | The owner took goods costing US\$360; no entry has been made. |

parts.label: (a)
parts.explanation: Opening inventory 8,900 + purchases (70,600 - 360 = 70,240) - closing inventory 12,300 = 66,840. Forgetting the goods taken gives 67,200.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Opening inventory 8,900 + purchases (70,600 - 360 = 70,240) - closing inventory 12,300 = 66,840. Forgetting the goods taken gives 67,200.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total charge for irrecoverable debts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.explanation: Gross profit 121,400 - 66,840 = 54,560. Expenses: wages 17,360, rent 5,100, insurance 1,620, depreciation 3,200, irrecoverable debts 730.40 = 28,010.40. Profit 26,549.60.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Gross profit 121,400 - 66,840 = 54,560. Expenses: wages 17,360, rent 5,100, insurance 1,620, depreciation 3,200, irrecoverable debts 730.40 = 28,010.40. Profit 26,549.60.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the capital at 31 December 2025 (opening capital + profit - total drawings).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the profit would be misstated if the owner's goods were not recorded as drawings.

points.description: Purchases would stay too high, so cost of sales is overstated and profit understated
Drawings and therefore the deduction from capital would be understated
Capital in the statement of financial position would be overstated

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: If the goods are left in purchases, cost of sales is too high and profit is understated by the cost of the goods. Drawings are also understated, so capital in the statement of financial position is overstated.

explanation: This item tests a trial balance with seven adjustments, profit and capital.
hints: Reduce purchases for the goods taken before finding cost of sales.
